Technology costs are modeled using past assumptions for demand response enabling technologies, as there are not generally products on the market that are currently able to respond to hourly price signals. We effectively are assuming that devices that have historically offered the ability for automate demand response will be enhanced to provide price responsive capabilities by 2030. Much of the potential occurs at very low to no costs, due to assumptions about natural adoption of such products (see “Technology Saturation” parameter described in the methods). Cost-benefit ratio across customer clusters for the 2030 low price forecast scenario; values below 1 are desirable, as they indicate that the technology has lower costs than benefits over its lifetime In addition to evaluating cost-effectiveness through a cost-benefit ratio, we apply a more stringent metric—short payback period—to assess the economic viability of different end-use responses. Specifically, we examine the potential for achieving a payback period of three years or less. Our findings, shown in Figure ES-7 for the aggregate system avoided costs metric, indicate that under fully dynamic pricing, nearly all customers and end uses meet this payback threshold. However, under medium or mild dynamic pricing, commercial cooling in particular has x a significant reduction in potential when held to this requirement. This distinction is critical when considering adoption trends. Historically, large commercial and industrial (C&I) customers have been the most active participants in demand response programs, demonstrating significant flexibility and responsiveness. If these energy-savvy customers are to become early adopters of dynamic pricing, tariffs would need to be structured in a way that makes participation economically favorable for them. Additionally, further research is needed to evaluate the price response potential of large C&I end uses beyond heating and cooling, such as industrial process loads, data center computations, water pumping and treatment beyond crop irrigation, which were not included in this study. For a typical Li-ion battery energy storage system (BESS), bill savings are possible, but highly dependent on the price design, as shown in Figure ES-8. But for many customers who are willing to invest in a BESS for other reasons (e.g. reliability), dynamic price arbitrage could offer an additional benefit to the customer and reduce the cost of such co-benefits. However, models that factor in the operation of the BESS for those co-benefits should be explored. For example, a BESS that has been purchased for reliability is unlikely to want to dispatch on the grid peak day, as that is the precise day that a customer might be worried about an outage.
